segments.text: And joining us on the show now is former Solicitor General of India Mr. Harish Salve.
Thank you very much sir for speaking to us.
Now even as the Supreme Court is now set to hear the case about illegal construction in Delhi, what is the ambit of

the kind of action that the Supreme Court can order because there are multiple laws that have been passed by the Parliament of India, the regularization of illegal colonies that has been done by the centre.
Can the Supreme Court order demolition, bypassing all these laws?
Well, first of all, this is nothing new.
I remember when Chief Justice Kirpal was there,
I was associated with some PILs when this issue came up.
In fact, he used to always tell the government you have in Delhi, the Republic of Sainikabad, not Sainik Farms.
And I'm relying on memory, so I could have some figures wrong.
I think over 40% of Delhi is illegal.
It may be worse now.
You know all your East Yamuna colonies and all that's completely illegal.
No norms have been followed.
Why do I blame the DDA?
I blame the DDA because after all Delhi has grown hugely in population.
Housing is a very basic need.
Food, housing and clothing are the three most basic needs.
and it can't only be for the slum dwellers who become world banks.

It has to be also for the middle class and the lower middle class people and that's where because your laws do not permit proper development then the mafias develop and when the mafias develop they do it purely for profit.
Now this is the vicious cycle and Justice Savarwal had appointed I remember Bhuralal's committee and this committee but then later on the Supreme Court itself diluted all those committees
So this is the reaction.
Now you have something big which has happened.
So I remember when it came up once there was a former Chief Justice, I don't want to name him.
He said this is not our job.
Now suddenly Supreme Court thinks it's a job.
Anyway, good.
What can the court direct?
The court can direct a lot because all these are, strictly speaking, illegal.
And you can have laws on the statute book.
You can enforce them.
But here again,
Today there is an illegal building.
If it belongs to a person who has made an illegal house and you go and demolish it.
If he is a mafia slumlord, demolish it by all means.
But if there is a building in which and you will see very large swaths of buildings.
Yes, if it is dangerous, you have to demolish it.
But how are we going to accommodate people who today live in illegal buildings?
Why have they had to buy illegal buildings?
Because illegal buildings are not available or affordable.
So it's a huge problem and this problem can't be resolved in courts.
The government has to at some point sit down and take a hard and firm look.
I am not for a minute suggesting that the rich and powerful who
thrown caution to the winds and made illegal homes should be spared.

But what about the lower middle class and the middle class people who for want of a better choice are today occupying a building which may not be entirely lawful or are living in a colony which is not lawful?
What are you going to do?
Throw them out and ask them to go and sleep on Delhi railway station?
You can't do that.
So, you know, this is what has happened is that the decrepit organizations
like DDA and MCD and all who have been running this as a scam.
I'm sorry to say I don't mince my words on this.
They have created a crisis and this crisis has to be resolved.
So yes, all illegal buildings must go.
But this building also was an illegal and unsafe building and putting our young students at risk.
But then students also need a place to stay.
Students are not staying there because they enjoyed living there.
I mean these are howls.
They are not even proper buildings.
Go around Delhi and see.
You are not supposed to use your basement for commercial purposes.
How many times have we had accidents because all these teaching shops run in basements?
What happened last time?
I think it was the Kejriwal government.
They made a lot of promises saying we are going to get all these out.
You live in Delhi now more than I do.
How much change have you seen on the ground?
But even if the court does step in, in 2006 there was large scale demolition of illegal buildings that was ordered by the court.
What happened?
Eventually a law was brought in by the Parliament of India which was extended year on year, decade on decade with the result that all of these illegal establishments still exist.
That's what I'm saying.
And then the court lost interest.
I'm sorry, I'm using strong words, the court lost interest because at some point the court said, well, this is not our job.

And now again, maybe because of this tragedy and considering the sensitivity of students now, in circumstances which is a conversation for another day, maybe the court feels that time has come where it has to take stock and see what's going on.
But I am on a more fundamental point, what are we going to do with this?
You have allowed
with all these yearly postponements and yearly this, the Buralal committee was unrelenting but then you dissolved all that and you thrown it all to the winds and this is where we are now.
So today you have to come up with a solution which is a driven by safety but b also tempered by reality.
And yes, find out if there is an illegal building, find out who made that illegal building, chase him, hunt him down, put him in jail.
But you can't throw people out on the street.
If it is unsafe, of course, you have to fix it.
You have to take time to fix it.
But this is what is going on.
And since this vicious circle has been in place for decades now, what do you think is a low-hanging fruit at this point?
What can be done?
Because in just the last three days, now we have the MCD telling us that about 52 illegal PG's or PG's in dilapidated state have been discovered in just a matter of three days.
Now if those 52 PG's are brought down, at least 520 children are going to be impacted.
Where will they go?
What's the possibility at this point?
That exactly is my point.
See, what happens is right now the MCD is trying to douse the fire.
A fire has been lit because the MCD's role has come into very sharp focus.
Everybody is saying what is going on in Delhi and the MCD is obviously at the receiving end because they have allowed all this to go on and they are partly responsible for all this.
Don't we all know what it takes to build a house in Delhi?
So, and I said this the other day also, why is it that building mafias have come up which have built structures?
The answer is very simple because an honest man, when he tries to make a building, gets so wrapped in the barbed wire of approvals.
The people who say, okay, I will manage are the people who manage to build buildings, but they are not the very nice type of people.

So, it is a rut which we have fallen into and then this grows but we have to make a distinction between middle class, lower middle class people who have gone, who have paid their hard-earned money to get these buildings and where they are living.
One of the things which we have been fighting for and I know I am digressing but it is directly connected with this.
What happens to all these illegal colonies?
They dump their sewage straight into the Yamuna.
That's why the Yamuna can never be cleaned.
So it's a larger problem.
You have to create a whole infrastructure.
It's not just one thing that you authorize buildings.
You have to then have today, you have to create a master plan.
And first of all, let's for a change have a master plan going forward.
Normally, by the time the DD announces the master plan, the decade is already over.
So it's after the end of the decade, they announce with retrospective effect what the law should have been for these 10 years.
Let's have a master plan going forward, which will recognize, which will do a complete survey of how many illegal buildings there are.
And believe me, with today's the technology available, it's not a big deal.

can all be done in weeks not even months identify the buildings get some town planners together to put their heads together come up with a master plan how do how many of these must go some of them will have to go because they are overclustered there is lack of sanitation etc etc how many of them can be preserved and yes please go and catch hold of the guys who made the buildings prosecute them send them to jail no problem but you can't
throw the baby out of the bath water.
You have to make accommodation available and this can't be done knee-jerk.
And this can't be done by a court-monitored committee.

You have to have a bunch of town planners sitting with policymakers in the government saying, okay, we have allowed this problem to fester and now it's gone from being a tennis ball to being a football, or maybe even bigger.
Okay, let's now see what's the way forward.
Mr. Salve, there are many people who seem to be losing patience with the rot that we see in our city and advocate taking a hammer to the problem.
You know, just level everything and not offer any kind of amnesty to anyone who has engaged in illegality.
Do you think that is at all possible?
It may sound drastic, it may even sound a little cruel.
Again I am telling you, when you say
No amnesty to anyone who is engaged in illegality.
Who is the man who is engaged in illegality?
The man who made a building with five flats, seven flats.
The man who made an illegal colony.
Those are the builders who have gone, grabbed government land or taken agricultural land, converted it without permission and gone and built them.
Please deal with them without remorse.
Or somebody who's built five floors instead of just three.
Correct.
But you have to have today a town plan going forward.
See today, when you make a town plan for a city, you are allowing three floors.
The family grows.
Over 20 years, the person will add two floors.
Now, did you anticipate the growth in population?
Have you created a situation where a middle class person could buy a second flat?

which was affordable and which was available and which was lawful you haven't yes now if your roads cannot take that kind of load some arrangement has to be made there has to be some time and you have to create an alternative facility and then tell people okay we are going to remove two of your floors but here is an alternative in three years time there will be 20 more buildings please
your extra usage, you have to move there and we are going to demolish.
It has to be a citizen's movement or rather citizens have to be on board with this.
You can't go to war on this.
And we have to recognize we have the powers that we have allowed this problem.
And yes, of course, political parties have changed and we've seen what has happened.
But the fact is today's government and today we have a very good government in Delhi.
But that government also can't say, OK, I'm oblivious to what has happened in the past because today you have a reality on your hands.
Yeah.
And I think you have to find a solution.
Who can find the solution?
You can't find it.
I can't find it.
I don't have a magic silver bullet by which you can solve this.
You have to have a set of town planners who put their head together and say, OK, this is the first identify the magnitude of the problem.
and then come up with a solution and that solution will be immediate, short term, medium term, long term.
And it may not be politically very popular, but ultimately and hopefully somebody will bite that bullet Mr. Harish Thal.
Today, when this has happened, you may get political consensus in India, you will never get because if the government says blue, the opposition today has to say green for the sake of saying it.
Unfortunately, we have lost any kind of collaborative politics today.

and we all see that if parliament can't work then I don't know how we are going to run India but I think we have to the government today will have the support of the citizenry when a thing like this has happened and the support of the citizenry is very important in making these changes.
Well let's hope that and thank you very much Mr Hari Salve for having shared your wisdom with us.
